title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation carried out through AI-generated content. Scammers produced a fabricated online article depicting a real public official and a real finance journalist conducting an interview that never took place, then used that article to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure is not one of a deployed AI product behaving unexpectedly, but of AI tools being applied deliberately outside any legitimate deployment context, to manufacture credible-seeming media at a scale and speed that would have been harder to achieve without them.

The scale reported by the regulator points to a systemic problem. A 182 percent rise in removed scams, and a pattern of fake websites, articles, reviews, and advertisements all constructed around impersonated public figures, indicates that content generation is now a low-friction step for fraudsters. Catching this kind of operation requires detection at the distribution layer, on the platforms and ad networks where the content appears, rather than at the point of content creation, because the generation itself leaves no single choke point.

What is not established is who produced the specific fake article, whether any particular AI system or service was used to create it, or whether any platform was found to have knowingly carried the material.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview never occurred but was designed to promote an illegitimate investment scheme. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common as artificial intelligence makes it easier for criminals to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians.

ASIC reports that AI-generated investment scams are rising significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, reviews, and advertisements featuring impersonated celebrities and politicians. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by financial commentators like Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through official registers before investing, warning that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
